stories.title: Is Jacobabad getting hotter?
stories.teaser: One of the hottest cities on Earth. The answer depends on what you measure.

steps.text: Jacobabad in Sindh, Pakistan, is one of the hottest cities on Earth. Start with the obvious question: is the average temperature going up? Look at the verdict and at the yearly dots.

The average mixes day and night. Split them: daytime highs on the left, night-time lows on the right. The nights are clearly getting warmer while the days are not. Warm nights make it harder for people to recover from the heat of the day.

stories.title: Same question, opposite answers
stories.teaser: Two hot cities, one in Pakistan and one in the USA. Their trends go opposite ways.

steps.text: Is the air getting more humid? In Lahore (left) humidity is clearly rising. In Phoenix, USA (right) it is clearly falling. The same variable can trend in opposite directions in two places, so a trend found in one place cannot be assumed everywhere.
Daytime highs show the same split: falling in Lahore, rising fast in Phoenix. We do not claim a cause here. The tool finds the change; explaining it is the next step for a detective.

stories.title: Too soon to tell: Hunza
stories.teaser: A trend that is not significant yet, and how many more years it would take.

steps.text: Hunza is in the Karakoram mountains of northern Pakistan. Are daytime highs rising? The rate is positive, but still small next to the normal ups and downs, so it is not significant yet. The tool estimates how many more years of data would settle it.
The average temperature, which includes the nights, is clearly rising. Not significant yet does not mean nothing is happening; it means this one measure needs a longer record.

stories.title: Greener from space
stories.teaser: The MODIS satellite sees central Lahore and a spot in the Thar desert getting greener.

steps.text: NDVI measures how green the land looks from NASA's Terra satellite (MODIS instrument). Each panel is a 5 km x 5 km window. Since 2000, both central Lahore (left) and a spot in the Thar desert (right) have become clearly greener.
